lang.thema: Black Friday: check an Amazon deal against its price in the month before
lang.titel: Black Friday – AMAZON DEAL OR DECOY? CHECK THE MONTH BEFORE
lang.text:
Your Black Friday bargain might cost more. A Groundwork Collaborative investigation checked Amazon's deal pages, and the results are brutal. But one pair of boots tells the story best.

This video answers one question: how do you check whether an Amazon Black Friday deal beat its own recent price? The report's headline says nearly 1 in 3 deals offered no savings to shoppers.

Start with the report's title: Deal or Decoy? Amazon's Deceptive Discounts. Its authors are Breyon Williams, Elizabeth Pancotti, and Lindsay Owens. They looked at products Amazon showcased as some of the best discounts of the year.

Here's the sample size. The analysis examined the prices of more than 350 products on Amazon's own deal pages for Black Friday and Cyber Monday in 2024 and 2025.

Now the first answer you can use. The report compares the sale price with the month before the sale. If the product sold for the same price or less then, the report calls it no real savings.

Be sure to like, share and save this video.

Amazon's Black Friday 2025 deals page says this. With so many deals to explore, we've handpicked some of the best ones you'll find. That's the promise the report tests. The report says these pages promote the deals as some of the best available.

The report's own sentence: the price of nearly 1 in 3 products Amazon described as deals was the same, or higher, during sale events than in the month leading up.

Some deals were worse. Across the past two years, nearly 1 in 10 advertised products cost more than in the month before.

Example one: yellow Hunter Women's Short Rain Boots, on sale for $126.99 on Black Friday 2025. The page says they had been $79.97 nine days before the sale event started.

Nine days. That's the whole gap between $79.97 and a deal at $126.99. The page spells it out: customers looking for a deal could have paid 59% more if they waited for the sale. Patience, punished.

Example two: men's UGG Butte boots, on sale for $179.98 on Cyber Monday 2025. The page says they were $98.40 roughly four weeks before the start of the sale event.

The report says that deal cost 83% more than the recent low. Notice the phrase recent low. It's the number to look for before you buy.

How bad is the typical bad case? The page says among these worse deals, the median sale-event price was 19% higher than what shoppers could have paid in the weeks before. Median means the middle value.

That leaves a practical question. How do you spot the gap before you buy? Here's a three-step check, built from the report's method. Step one: write down the sale price shown on the deal.

Step two: find what the same product cost in the month leading up to the sale. The report uses that month as its comparison.

Step three: compare. A month-before price the same or lower than the sale price means no real savings, in the report's terms. If the sale price is higher, that's one of the worse deals.

Run it on the Hunter boots. Sale price $126.99, nine days before $79.97. The sale price is higher, so that's a worse deal under this check.

Run it on the UGG boots too. Sale price $179.98, roughly four weeks before $98.40. Same result: higher during the sale. Not a great look for a bargain.

How far back does the check look? The page's phrase is the month leading up to the sale. Its two boot examples look back nine days and roughly four weeks. Notice the window. Both boot examples show a gap within a month of price history.

Same price isn't a loss. It's just not a saving, and that's what the report counts as no real savings.

Deal or Decoy calls on federal and state regulators to crack down on misleading discounts. It also wants retailers to show the lowest price a product sold for in the previous 30 days when advertising a sale.

That's close to the check you just ran by hand: the sale price against the month before.

Here's a twist. Since learning of the study, Amazon has removed the deal pages the study drew from.

But the report links archived versions. Black Friday 2024, Cyber Monday 2024, Black Friday 2025 and Cyber Monday 2025. Four links, four sale events.

This check needs two prices and some arithmetic. The earlier price is the part you have to find.

Owens says: Millions of Americans wait all year for Black Friday and Cyber Monday to score the biggest bargains on stocking stuffers and household staples. Owens adds: Amazon dominates online shopping, and families count on its sale events to stretch their dollars.

How many people does this touch? The page says a record 203 million Americans shopped between Thanksgiving and Cyber Monday in 2025. It adds that this year, 70% of U.S. customers plan to take advantage of holiday promotions.

Co-author Lindsay Owens is quoted saying shoppers who wait for these major sale events may be playing rip-off roulette. That's a reaction, not a verdict on every deal. Lindsay Owens is listed as Groundwork Collaborative's President and CEO and a report co-author.

Another line from Owens: shoppers deserve to know they can trust every deal Amazon promises them. Until then, the check is yours to run.

Now the limits. The analysis covers more than 350 products from Amazon's own deal pages. That's the deals Amazon showcased, not every price on Amazon.

The 1 in 3 figure is about deals on those pages in 2024 and 2025. It doesn't say what any single product will cost this year.

The numbers are Groundwork Collaborative's own analysis of hundreds of these deals. The page links archived copies of the deal pages, so you can look at the originals.

The title uses strong words, decoy and deceptive. This video repeats only the measured comparison: sale price against the month before. Real savings, in this report, means compared with the month before. It's one comparison, not the only possible one.

In December 2025, Groundwork teamed up with Consumer Reports and More Perfect Union on Instacart prices. The page says the findings triggered investigations by the Federal Trade Commission and New York Attorney General.

Quick recap. Compare the sale price with the month before. Same or lower earlier means no real savings. Higher during the sale means a worse deal. Now a hypothetical, not our test. Say you run a small online shop and plan a holiday sale. Before you mark anything as a deal, compare it with the lowest price in the previous 30 days.

This is a hypothetical habit, not legal or financial advice. The report asks regulators to require it; it doesn't say that rule exists today.

Another hypothetical: you write a deals roundup for a client. Before listing a deal, compare its price with the month before. The report did that for more than 350 products. No income claim here. It's simply a habit that keeps your claims checkable.

So, how do you check a Black Friday deal on Amazon? Write down the sale price. Then find the price from the month before.

Hunter boots: $79.97 nine days earlier, $126.99 on Black Friday 2025. UGG boots: $98.40 about four weeks earlier, $179.98 on Cyber Monday 2025.

Nearly 1 in 3 deals on Amazon's own pages failed that test in 2024 and 2025. Those are the report's numbers, for those pages, in those two years.

Next time a banner shouts best deal, ask one question first. Is this price better than last month's? And if you write or sell deals for a living, the same check keeps your claims honest. That's the click. A banner is a claim, and now you know the comparison that tests it.
